result:
There used to be a distinct magic in unfolding a paper map on the hood of a car, trying to decipher the blue veins of highways while the wind fought to tear the creases apart. Today, a glowing blue dot follows us everywhere, persistently anchoring us to certainty. We know precisely how many minutes stand between us and our destination, down to the crimson smear of a traffic jam three miles ahead. Efficiency has won, and in its victory, we have quietly surrendered the art of getting lost.

Getting lost used to be a rite of passage. Taking a wrong turn never triggered an immediate, robotic voice calmly insisting that we make an instant turnaround. Instead, a wrong turn was an unscheduled prologue. It led to weathered diners with pie spinning lazily in glass cases, to overgrown orchards humming with cicadas, or to sudden, breathtaking overlooks that no algorithm would ever deem optimal. Being lost forced us to pay attention. Without a satellite whispering instructions, we had to read the tilt of the shadows, scan faded street signs, and commit the cardinal sin of modern travel: rolling down the window to ask a stranger for directions.

I have no desire to throw my smartphone into the ocean, of course. Convenience undeniably has its charms. Yet every now and then, I deliberately ignore the glowing purple route. I turn down an unpaved country road just to see where the green canopy closes in, chasing the quiet, forgotten thrill of being unfound.
